# Module II: Dealing with internal boundaries

::: {.section-topics}
Structured meshes – Immersed Boundary Method – OBSTs in FDS.

Unstructured meshes.

FFT and ULMAT (PARDISO, HYPRE) Poisson Solvers – local single mesh. Velocity error in internal boundaries.

Example 1: Single mesh case.

Unstructured discretization via cut-cell method - GEOMs in FDS.

Unstructured Poisson solve on cut cells.

Example 2: Mass balance for sphere source.

## Structured meshes – Immersed Boundary Method {.ibm-intro-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Boundary representation in structured meshes: Immersed boundary methods\*
:::

::: {.body}
- The presence of the body in Cartesian grid is accounted for using a forcing function.
- Equations for grid points next to or at the boundary are given a special RHS, such that the velocity BC is approximated.
:::

::: {.force}
Immersed Boundary Force defined in:

- Continuous governing equations^+^: IBM.
- Discrete governing equations^o,x,^^: Discrete Forcing IBM.
:::

::: {.force2}
Force is:

- Computed on surface and spread on surrounding points^+,x^: Diffuse Interface IBM.
- Computed for each neighboring Cartesian point in the gas phase^o,#^: Sharp interface IBM.
:::

::: {.fig .fit}

:::

## Structured meshes – Immersed Boundary Method {.ibm-obst-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.body}
In FDS OBSTs surfaces are snapped to fluid grid:

- Solve for H everywhere, IBM on [normal velocity components]{style='color:#ff0000'}.
- Assume in forcing point [$p$]{style='color:#ff0000'} we have an approximation to normal velocity $u^{n+1}=u^{d}$
:::

::: {.obst}
`&OBST XB=1.5,1.7,-0.8,0.8,-0.8,0.4 SURF_ID=… /`{style='color:#ff0000'}
:::

::: {.eq1}
$$(F_{A}+F_{B})^{n} =- \frac{u^{d}- u^{n}}{\Delta t}- \frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x}$$
:::

::: {.lab-body}
[Body Force at p.]{style='color:#ff0000'}
:::

::: {.iter}
But we don't know $H$, we still can iterate in k the projection:
:::

::: {.eq2}
$$(F_{A}+F_{B})^{n,k} =- \frac{u^{d}- u^{n}}{\Delta t}- \left.\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x}\right.^{k-1}$$
:::

::: {.lg-h}
$H$
:::

::: {.lg-ibm}
IBM
:::

::: {.lg-wm}
WM Stress
:::

::: {.lg-tv}
Tangential Velocity
:::

::: {.sym-u}
$u$
:::

::: {.sym-p}
$p$
:::

::: {.eqpoisson}
$$\nabla^{2}H^{k} =- \left[ \frac{\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{th,n+1}- \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}^{n}}{\Delta t}+\nabla \cdot (\mathbf{F}_{A}+\mathbf{F}_{B})^{n,k} \right]$$
:::

::: {.eq3}
$$u^{n+1,k} =u^{n}- \Delta t\left[ (F_{A}+F_{B})^{n,k}+\left.\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x}\right.^{k} \right]$$
:::

::: {.conv}
Up to convergence [$\left| u^{n+1,k}- u^{d} \right|<\varepsilon$]{style='color:#ff0000'} (velocity error tolerance).

Use of one iteration is common in IBM codes.
:::

:::

## Unstructured meshes {.ib-unstructured-bc-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.body}
- Solve for **H only on gas** phase cells. Apply [boundary condition for H]{style='color:#ff0000'} in internal boundaries.
- We know the end of step normal velocity $u^{n+1}=u^{d}$
:::

::: {.li1 .dash-item}
Set Homogeneous Neumann BC at boundary points:
:::

::: {.eqn1}
$$\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x}=0$$
:::

::: {.li2 .dash-item}
Also, at boundary point set:
:::

::: {.eqn2}
$$(F_{A}+F_{B})^{n} =- \frac{u^{d}- u^{n}}{\Delta t}$$
:::

::: {.li3 .dash-item}
Final velocity in Boundary:
:::

::: {.eqn3}
$$u^{n+1} =u^{n}- \Delta t\left[ (F_{A}+F_{B})^{n}+\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x} \right]$$
:::

::: {.strike .fit}
<svg viewBox="0 0 76.2 118.8" role="img" aria-label="Red arrow striking out the pressure gradient term.">
<line x1="0.0" y1="118.8" x2="76.2" y2="0.0" stroke="#ff0000" stroke-width="4.17"/>
<polygon points="76.2 0.0, 75.2 14.2, 63.6 6.8" fill="#ff0000"/>
</svg>
:::

::: {.zero}
$0$
:::

::: {.eqn4}
$$u^{n+1} =u^{n}- \Delta t\left[ - \frac{u^{d}- u^{n}}{\Delta t} \right]=u^{d}$$
:::

::: {.lg-h}
$H$
:::

::: {.lg-nv}
Normal Velocity
:::

::: {.lg-wm}
WM Stress
:::

::: {.lg-tv}
Tangential Velocity
:::

::: {.eqn5}
$$\frac{\Delta H}{\Delta x}=0$$

Final velocity is equal to prescribed velocity.

Allows for flow acceleration.

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric transform Solver FFT:
:::

- Structured mesh in a Box. Same Boundary conditions for H on each side of the Box.
- Discrete Poisson operator is separable.
:::

::: {.fig}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-023-picture-01.png){fig-alt="Structured box mesh with the same boundary condition on every side."}

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.fft-eigen-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric transform Solver FFT:
:::

::: {.body}
Assume discretized system symmetric positive definite (SPD):
:::

::: {.eq1}
$$\mathbf{A}_{N\times N}\boldsymbol{H}_{N\times 1} =\boldsymbol{R}_{N\times 1}$$
:::

::: {.body2}
Method of solution using Eigenvalues/Eigenvectors, [imagine I have them]{style='color:#ff0000'}:
:::

::: {.eq2}
$$\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{i},N\times 1} =\lambda_{i}\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{i},N\times 1}$$
:::

::: {.lab1}
Eigenvalue problem.
:::

::: {.eq3}
$$\lambda_{i},\ i=1,\dots ,N$$
:::

::: {.lab2}
Eigenvalues, all real, same sign (SPD).
:::

::: {.eq4}
$$\boldsymbol{q}_{\boldsymbol{i},N\times 1},\ i=1,\dots ,N$$
:::

::: {.lab3}
Corresponding eigenvectors, real (SPD).
:::

::: {.ask}
How would I use them to solve my Poisson equation linear system?
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.fft-eigendecomp-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric transform Solver FFT:
:::

::: {.body}
Stack the eigenvectors in columns of a matrix:
:::

::: {.eqQ}
$$\mathbf{Q}_{N\times N}=\left[ \begin{matrix} \boldsymbol{q}_{1} & \dots & \boldsymbol{q}_{N} \end{matrix} \right]$$
:::

::: {.withprop}
with property
:::

::: {.eqOrth}
$$\mathbf{Q}^{-1}=\mathbf{Q}^{T}$$
:::

::: {.recast}
Recast for all $\lambda_{i}$'s:
:::

::: {.eqBig}
$$\left[ \begin{matrix} a_{11} & \cdots & a_{1N} \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ a_{N1} & \cdots & a_{NN} \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} \boldsymbol{q}_{1} & \boldsymbol{q}_{2} & \cdots & \boldsymbol{q}_{N} \end{matrix} \right]=\left[ \begin{matrix} \boldsymbol{q}_{1} & \boldsymbol{q}_{2} & \cdots & \boldsymbol{q}_{N} \end{matrix} \right]\left[ \begin{matrix} \lambda_{1} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & \lambda_{N} \end{matrix} \right]$$
:::

::: {.aq-a}
$\mathbf{A}$
:::

::: {.aq-q1}
$\mathbf{Q}$
:::

::: {.aq-eq}
$=$
:::

::: {.aq-q2}
$\mathbf{Q}$
:::

::: {.aq-l}
$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$
:::

::: {.orlab}
or
:::

::: {.eqFact}
$$\mathbf{A} =\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{T}$$
:::

::: {.wherelab}
where
:::

::: {.eqLam}
$$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{N\times N}=\left[ \begin{matrix} \lambda_{1} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & \lambda_{N} \end{matrix} \right]$$
:::

::: {.lamlab}
Eigenvalue diagonal matrix.
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.fft-transform-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric transform Solver FFT:
:::

::: {.back .dash-item}
Back to our linear system:
:::

::: {.eqAH}
$$\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.recast .dash-item}
Recast for all $\lambda_{i}$'s:
:::

::: {.eqAQ}
$$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{Q} =\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}$$
:::

::: {.eqQLQ}
$$\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.wherelab}
where
:::

::: {.eqLam}
$$\boldsymbol{\Lambda}_{N\times N}=\left[ \begin{matrix} \lambda_{1} & \cdots & 0 \\ \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ 0 & \cdots & \lambda_{N} \end{matrix} \right]$$
:::

::: {.orlab}
or
:::

::: {.eqLQ}
$$\textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{H}=\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.acts}
$\mathbf{Q}^{T}$ acts as a linear transformation:
:::

::: {.eqHhat}
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}=\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{H}$$
:::

::: {.comma}
,
:::

::: {.eqRhat}
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}=\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.modal}
Solution and RHS in transformed space (modal, wave space).
:::

::: {.inlab}
In transformed space:
:::

::: {.eqDiag}
$$\textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$$
:::

::: {.cheap}
System is diagonal! Very cheap to solve!
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.fft-procedure-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric transform Solver FFT:
:::

::: {.body .dash-item}
Procedure using Eigendecomposition:
:::

::: {.step1}
1. Compute
:::

::: {.eq1}
$$\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}=\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}^{T}}\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.cost1}
, cost $N^{2}$ FP multiplications
:::

::: {.step2}
2. Compute
:::

::: {.eq2}
$$\textcolor{red}{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}=\hat{\boldsymbol{R}}$$
:::

::: {.cost2}
, cost $N$ FP divisions
:::

::: {.step3}
3. Compute
:::

::: {.eq3}
$$\boldsymbol{H}=\textcolor{red}{\mathbf{Q}}\hat{\boldsymbol{H}}$$
:::

::: {.cost3}
, cost $N^{2}$ FP multiplications
:::

::: {.need}
Need to get eigen values/vectors and eigenvector matrix is full.
:::

::: {.note}
- For our matrix Eigenvectors and eigenvalues can be defined analytically.
- We never build $\mathbf{A}$.
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.fft-cost-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Fast trigonometric Solver FFT\*:
:::

::: {.body}
- The [$\mathbf{Q}^{T}$]{style='color:#ff0000'} transformation entries are the same as the basis of a [forward 2D or 3D trigonometric transform]{style='color:#ff0000'} (discrete sine, cosine, real Fourier transform).
- The [$\mathbf{Q}$]{style='color:#ff0000'} product is equivalent to an [inverse 2D or 3D trigonometric transform]{style='color:#ff0000'}.
:::

::: {.body3}
- [Fast Trigonometric transforms can be used]{style='color:#ff0000'} reducing the cost to:
:::

::: {.c2d}
2D: $N=N_{x}\times N_{y}$, cost from $\textcolor{red}{2}\textcolor{#0070c0}{N^{2}}\textcolor{red}{+N}$ FPs down to $\textcolor{red}{2}\textcolor{#0070c0}{N\left( \log \left( N_{x} \right)+\log \left( N_{y} \right) \right)}\textcolor{red}{+N}$
:::

::: {.c3d}
3D: $N=N_{x}\times N_{y}\times N_{z}$, cost from $\textcolor{red}{2}\textcolor{#0070c0}{N^{2}}\textcolor{red}{+N}$ FPs down to $\textcolor{red}{2}\textcolor{#0070c0}{N\left( \log \left( N_{x} \right)+\log \left( N_{y} \right)+\log \left( N_{z} \right) \right)}\textcolor{red}{+N}$
:::

::: {.punch}
Fast trigonometric Solvers are the most efficient Poisson solvers for block-structured grids!
:::

::: {.refs}
\*<https://github.com/NCAR/NCAR-Classic-Libraries-for-Geophysics/tree/main/FishPack>
:::

:::

## Running the class examples {.run-examples-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Every example is run the same way:
:::

::: {.steps}
1. **Go to the case:** `cd 04_Pressure/Cases/example_1`
2. **Pick the solver:** leave one `&PRES` line active in `Example_1.fds`.\
   [Examples 4–5 have one input file per solver instead.]{.aside}
3. **Copy the input into `results/`, named for the solver:**\
   `cp Example_1.fds results/Example_1_FFT.fds`\
   `cd results`, set [`CHID`]{.red}`='Example_1_FFT'` — **[don't forget!]{.red}**
4. **Run it, one MPI process per mesh:**\
   `mpirun -n 1 fds Example_1_FFT.fds`
5. **Look at it:** `Example_1_FFT.out`; `smokeview Example_1_FFT` from `results/`; `python eval.py` from the case directory for the plots.
:::

::: {.shortcut}
*macOS / Linux: `./run.sh FFT` does steps 3 and 4, and stops if the active `&PRES` line is not the one you named.*

*Windows: the same steps in the CMDfds prompt, `copy` for `cp` and `mpiexec` for `mpirun`.*
:::

::: {.sub-head2}
Each case directory:
:::

::: {.tree}
<pre>example_1/
  Example_1.fds   <span>the input</span>
  README.md       <span>exact steps, what to look for</span>
  run.sh          <span>steps 3–4 for you</span>
  eval.py         <span>plots, into plots/</span>
  results/        <span>your runs</span>
  reference/      <span>our runs, made before class</span></pre>
:::

::: {.tbl .cases}
| Case | MPI `-n` | Runs in class? |
|---|---|---|
| `example_1` | 1 | yes, seconds |
| `example_2` | 1 | yes, seconds |
| `example_3` | 8 | yes, minutes |
| `example_4` | 16 | no, cluster |
| `example_5` | 8 | no, hours |
:::

::: {.fallback}
No run of your own? `eval.py` falls back to `reference/`, so every figure can be made on a laptop.
:::

:::

## Some important &PRES parameters: {.pres-params-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.body}
- `&PRES SOLVER defines which Poisson solver to use (FFT,ULMAT,UGLMAT).`{style='color:#ff0000'}
:::

::: {.tbl}
| Namelist | Parameter | Default | Unit | Usage |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `&PRES` | `VELOCITY_TOLERANCE` | dx/2 | m/s | Requested tolerance for velocity error. |
| | `MAX_PRESSURE_ITERATIONS` | 10 | | Max number allowed for pressure iterations. |
| | `SUSPEND_PRESSURE_ITERATIONS` | F | | Suspend iterations if progress too slow? |
| | `ITERATION_SUSPEND_FACTOR` | 0.95 | | Suspend is new velocity is not smaller than this value of the old. |
| | `PRESSURE_TOLERANCE` | 20/dx² | s⁻² | Tolerance for inseparable pressure equation residual. |
| | `TUNNEL_PRECONDITIONER` | F | | Use tunnel preconditioner? |
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.ulmat-intro-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
ULMAT PARDISO (Unstructured Local Matrix Solver)
:::

::: {.body}
- Unstructured mesh. Only solve in gas cells, per mesh.
- We use PARDISO from Intel Math Kernel Library (MKL). Cholesky decomposition\* of sparse A.
- One matrix A per pressure zone in the mesh.
:::

::: {.fig}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-034-picture-01.png){fig-alt="Sparsity of A alongside its Cholesky factor L, which has many more non-zero entries."}
:::

::: {.arr-a}
<svg viewBox="0 0 12.80 28.80" width="100%" style="overflow:visible;display:block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true"><defs><marker id="ar34a" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="10" refY="5" markerWidth="4" markerHeight="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#156082"/></marker></defs><line x1="6.40" y1="28.80" x2="6.40" y2="0.00" stroke="#156082" stroke-width="2.50" marker-end="url(#ar34a)"/></svg>
:::

::: {.arr-l}
<svg viewBox="0 0 12.80 28.80" width="100%" style="overflow:visible;display:block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true"><defs><marker id="ar34b" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="10" refY="5" markerWidth="4" markerHeight="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#156082"/></marker></defs><line x1="6.40" y1="28.80" x2="6.40" y2="0.00" stroke="#156082" stroke-width="2.50" marker-end="url(#ar34b)"/></svg>
:::

::: {.arr-sym}
<svg viewBox="0 0 12.80 28.80" width="100%" style="overflow:visible;display:block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true"><defs><marker id="ar34c" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="10" refY="5" markerWidth="4" markerHeight="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#156082"/></marker></defs><line x1="6.40" y1="28.80" x2="6.40" y2="0.00" stroke="#156082" stroke-width="2.50" marker-end="url(#ar34c)"/></svg>
:::

::: {.lab-a}
Very Sparse, has constant coefficients.
:::

::: {.lab-l}
Lower triangular, much more non-zero entries than A.
:::

::: {.lab-sym}
A symmetric, $U=L^{T}$
:::

::: {.refs}
\* T. Davis, "Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems," SIAM (2006). J. Saad, "Iterative Methods for Sparse Linear Systems," 2nd Ed, SIAM (2003).
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.ulmat-solve-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
ULMAT PARDISO (Unstructured Local Matrix Solver)
:::

::: {.body}
- Factorization only needs to be done at setup time. Most expensive part.
- Only solve phase needs to be called when time stepping.
:::

::: {.back .dash-item}
Back to our linear system:
:::

::: {.eqAH}
$$\mathbf{A}\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.fromfac}
From factorization:
:::

::: {.eqLL}
$$\mathbf{L}\mathbf{L}^{T}\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.solve}
Solve Phase:
:::

::: {.n1}
1.
:::

::: {.eq1}
$$\mathbf{L}\boldsymbol{Y}=\boldsymbol{R}$$
:::

::: {.lab1}
Forward Substitution cost of the order of non-zeros in L
:::

::: {.n2}
2.
:::

::: {.eq2}
$$\mathbf{L}^{T}\boldsymbol{H}=\boldsymbol{Y}$$
:::

::: {.lab2}
Backward Substitution of the order of non-zeros in L
:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers {.hypre-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
ULMAT HYPRE (Unstructured Local Matrix Solver)
:::

::: {.body}
- Unstructured mesh. Only solve in gas cells, per mesh.
- We use Conjugate Gradient iterative algorithm from HYPRE library.
- Algebraic Multigrid Preconditioner.
- One matrix A per pressure zone in each mesh.
- Memory usage ~5-8 Number of non-zeros in matrix A.
:::

::: {.body2}
- Solution is essentially the same as with LU.
- Solver can be slower than ULMAT PARDISO.
- Memory: much more scalable for large problems.
:::

::: {.fig}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-039-picture-01.png){fig-alt="HYPRE library documentation page."}
:::

::: {.refs}
<https://hypre.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html>
:::

:::

## Local Single Mesh Poisson Solvers Recap: {.solver-recap-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.body}
**FFT:**

- Exploits the space of solutions of the Poisson Equation.
- Makes use of Fast trigonometric transforms.
- Works with simple logically cartesian grids.
- Fastest algorithm.
- For internal boundaries (OBSTS) requires iteration to reduce velocity error.

**ULMAT PARDISO:**

- Solves only on gas cells.
- Factors the Poisson Matrix using Cholesky decomposition.
- Fast for small number of cells.
- Factorization matrix can require a lot of memory to store and use.

**ULMAT HYPRE:**

- Solves only on gas cells.
- Iterative Method from HYPRE library.
- Slower than the previous for small number of cells.
- Memory efficient, only option when PARDISO not available to compile FDS (ARM Mac builds).
:::

:::

## Unstructured meshes – Cut-cell method for geometries {.cutcell-intro-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Boundary conforming: Cut-cell (embedded boundary) methods\*
:::

::: {.body}
- Structured Cartesian mesh acts as background regular mesh, cut-cell polyhedra defined where geometry intersects grid.
- We cut-off the mesh outside of the solution domain (for us the gas phase).
- We are left with discretizing governing equations in cut-cell region.
:::

::: {.fig-l}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-042-picture-01.png){fig-alt="Sphere geometry embedded in a background Cartesian mesh."}
:::

::: {.box-detail}

:::

:::

::: {.fig-r}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-042-picture-03.png){fig-alt="Close-up where the geometry crosses the grid: yellow cut-cell polyhedra against the structured cells, with a small cell circled."}
:::

::: {.refs}
\* M. Berger, "Cut Cells: Meshes and Solvers," *Handbook of Numerical Analysis* **18** (2017).
:::

## Unstructured meshes – Cut-cell method for geometries {.cutcell-prosecons-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Advantages:
:::

::: {.adv}
- Well suited for conservative discretization (volumes and boundaries well defined).
- Complexity remains local to geometry surface.
- Cost of grid generation is buried in work to define cut-cells. Burden on surface meshing.
- Body surface mesh can be of different size than Cartesian grid.
- We have efficient cut-cell computation schemes.
- Resulting meshes are computationally efficient, most cells are regular.
:::

::: {.sub-head2}
Disadvantages:
:::

::: {.dis}
- Cut-cells are very irregular polyhedra.
- Stability/conditioning issues due to small cut-cells (explicit time integration, linear system solution).
- Can't define boundary layer meshes close to body (like chimera/overset meshes).
- Wall modeled IBM is an open problem, we have to stick to unstructured projection and expensive Poisson solvers.
:::

::: {.fig-t}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-043-picture-01.png){fig-alt="Smokeview view of a tetrahedron GEOM inside the mesh, its faces coloured by SURF: red, blue and grey."}
:::

::: {.fig-b .fit}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-043-picture-02.png){fig-alt="FDS input for the tetrahedron: three &SURF lines and a &GEOM with VERTS and FACES."}
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
The three slides that follow -- the finite volume discretization and the small-cell treatment -- are for a longer sitting. If time is short, go straight from here to the unstructured Poisson solve.
:::

## Unstructured meshes – Cut-cell method for geometries {.smallcell-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Treatment of small cells (explicit time integration):
:::

::: {.body}
Cut cell methods lead to **small** irregular cells, which penalize the time step size on explicit time integration.
:::

::: {.lit}
Literature: (a) **Cell merging**\*, **cell linking**^+^ or **cell mixing**^#^ schemes.
:::

::: {.fig}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-046-panels.png){fig-alt="Three panels of the same cut cell region. (a) a small gas-phase cut cell ii shaded against the solid; (b) the same cell marked SLAVE linked to the larger MASTER cell above it; (c) three candidate target cells a small cell could be linked to, each with an arrow from the small cell."}
:::

::: {.note}
- **We link small cells to large surrounding cells at the discrete equation level.**
- **Size threshold for cells to be merged is given by `&MISC CCVOL_LINK` (0.5 default)**
- Simply assign same unknown number to small and large cell.
- Volume and flux terms will add for said unknown, cancelling out in shared faces.
:::

::: {.refs}
\*T. Ye, R. Mittal, H.S. Udaykumar, W. Shyy. *J. Comput. Phys.* **156** pp 209-240 (1999).<br>
+ M. P. Kirkpatrick, S. W. Armfield, J. H. Kent. *J. Comput. Phys.* **184** pp 1-36 (2003).<br>
\# M. Meyer, A. Devesa, S. Hickel, X. Y. Hu, N. A. Adams. *J. Comput. Phys.* **229** pp 6300-6317 (2010).
:::

:::

::: {.notes}
Last of the optional three. CCVOL_LINK comes back in Example 2 as the bonus exercise, so it is worth a word even when this slide is skipped.
:::

## Unstructured meshes – Cut-cell method for geometries {.cc-poisson-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Consider LHS of Poisson Eq. for H integrated on a cell:
:::

::: {.eq1}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-047-picture-01.svg){fig-alt="Left-hand side of the Poisson equation integrated over a cut cell."}
:::

::: {.approx}
Approximate:
:::

::: {.eq2}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-047-picture-02.svg){fig-alt="Approximated face gradient."}
:::

::: {.withlab}
With $\Delta x_{i}$ cell centroid to centroid distance in direction *i*.
:::

::: {.fig}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-047-faces.png){fig-alt="A curved solid cutting a Cartesian grid. Orange segments join the centroids of regular face pairs, blue segments join the centroids either side of a cut face or a regular-to-cut face."}
:::

::: {.steps}
Steps:

1. Build unstructured finite volume discretization matrix for H (face by face).
2. Invoke [unstructured linear system solver]{style='color:#ff0000'} setup (default [UGLMAT&nbsp;HYPRE]{style='color:#ff0000'} for a single pressure zone, [ULMAT&nbsp;PARDISO]{style='color:#ff0000'} when there is more than one). Note we can't use FFT, why?
3. In time marching build unstructured Poisson RHS and call [unstructured solver]{style='color:#ff0000'} when needed.
:::

:::

## Example 2: Mass balance for sphere source. {.ex2-input-slide}

::: {.slide-layout}

::: {.sub-head}
Sphere blowing Propane (isothermal flow):
:::

::: {.file}
**FDS Input file:** `Example_2.fds`
:::

::: {.body}
**Study the input file, then run it** with steps **[3–4]{style='color:#ff0000'}** of [*Running the class examples*](#running-the-class-examples), keeping `CHID='Example_2'`:

- The solver is set to `&PRES SOLVER='ULMAT PARDISO'`: why not FFT? The `ULMAT`/`UGLMAT` variants are commented out below it — try them.
- How is our tracer defined? What species is it composed of?
- How is the specified mass flux on sphere GEOM defined?
- Devices, mass balance:
    - How do we account for tracer mass into the domain?
    - How do we add the tracer mass that leaves the domain?
    - How do we get the remaining tracer mass in the domain?
:::

::: {.pid}
**PID (Proportional Integral Derivative) Control:**
:::

::: {.fig-pid}
![](Section_2_assets/slide-048-picture-01.png){fig-alt="The PID control expression: output as a proportional gain times the error, plus an integral gain times the error integrated over time, plus a derivative gain times the rate of change of the error."}
:::

::: {.arr-p}
<svg viewBox="0 0 28.32 14.76" width="100%" style="overflow:visible;display:block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" aria-hidden="true"><defs><marker id="s48p" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="10" refY="5" markerWidth="4" markerHeight="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L10,5 L0,10 z" fill="#156082"/></marker></defs><line x1="0.00" y1="14.76" x2="28.32" y2="0.00" stroke="#156082" stroke-width="2.50" marker-end="url(#s48p)"/></svg>
